claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of multi-element nanoparticles is governed primarily by lattice strain induced by atomic-size mismatch.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch reduces local lattice distortion.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch promotes a more uniform solid-solution structure.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch slows atomic diffusion.
Slower atomic diffusion helps preserve single-phase chemical and structural integrity.
Atomic-size differences among constituent elements generate local lattice strain fields.
Lower lattice strain elevates kinetic barriers for atomic diffusion.
Kinetic hindrance of atomic diffusion delays thermally activated phase segregation.
Kinetic hindrance of atomic diffusion delays nanoparticle sintering.
Nanoparticles with minimized atomic-size mismatch will undergo less phase segregation than nanoparticles with larger size disparities during high-temperature service.
Nanoparticles with minimized atomic-size mismatch will undergo less sintering and coarsening than nanoparticles with larger size disparities during high-temperature service.
The proposed size-mismatch mechanism requires the constituent elements to remain within their solubility limits.
The proposed mechanism requires enough thermal activation to promote diffusion.
Surface encapsulation or oxidation can dominate stabilization and obscure the effect of atomic-size mismatch.
Strong intermetallic interactions or extreme processing conditions can reduce the influence of atomic-size mismatch on stability.
Surface effects, synthesis history, and service atmosphere can influence diffusion rates and phase-segregation kinetics.
